cues.text: A point in three dimensional Cartesian space is an ordered triple x, y, z.
The coordinates measure signed positions along three mutually perpendicular
axes with a common length scale.
The order matters: interchanging coordinates generally changes the point.
The distance from the origin to the point is square root of x squared plus y
squared plus z squared.
This follows by applying the Pythagorean theorem first in a coordinate plane
and then to the remaining perpendicular direction.
For the point two, negative three, six, the squared distance is four plus nine
plus thirty six, or forty nine, giving distance seven.
A negative coordinate changes the location but does not make a distance
negative.
A point with one coordinate zero lies on the corresponding coordinate plane.
A point with two coordinates zero lies on an axis.
Points with no zero coordinate belong to one of eight octants according to
their three signs.
The numbering of octants can depend on convention, so a sign description is
unambiguous.
A flat drawing of space is only a projection; do not measure angles or lengths
directly from a slanted sketch.
The distance between two space points is the length of their coordinate
difference.
Subtract the first point's x, y and z coordinates from the corresponding
coordinates of the second, square the three differences, add and take the
nonnegative root.
For A at one, two, three and B at three, negative one, nine, the difference is
two, negative three, six.
The distance is seven.
Reversing A and B reverses every component but preserves the distance.
Coordinate projections give another useful interpretation.
The perpendicular projection of B onto the x y coordinate plane is three,
negative one, zero.
Only z is replaced by zero, because the perpendicular direction is along the z
axis.
Its distance from that plane is absolute z, or nine.
Projection onto an axis sets the other two coordinates to zero, and the
distance to that axis uses those two removed coordinates.
For example, the distance from B to the z axis is square root of ten.
Keep a projected point, a projected displacement and a distance distinct: they
are different kinds of objects, even when they arise from the same coordinate
calculation.
The section formula works component by component in space.
If P divides A B internally with A P to P B equal to positive m to n, then
its position is the quantity n A plus m B divided by m plus n.
The notation abbreviates the same weighted calculation in each of the three
coordinates.
With A at zero, zero, zero and B at six, three, nine, internal ratio two to
one
gives four, two, six.
The larger weight belongs to B because P is nearer B.
Equal positive weights give the midpoint, three, three halves, nine halves.
External division uses the quantity m B minus n A divided by m minus n,
provided m is not n.
External ratio two to one gives twelve, six, eighteen, beyond B.
For distinct endpoints, equal external distances do not give a finite point.
Check collinearity as well as the ratio by seeing that the displacement to P
is
a scalar multiple of the endpoint displacement.
The internal formula also applies to a line segment parameter between zero and
one; a parameter outside that range describes a point on an extension.
A line direction in space can be represented by a nonzero triple of direction
ratios.
For a line through two distinct points, their coordinate differences give such
a triple.
The ratios need not have length one.
Multiplying all three by a nonzero scalar preserves the underlying unoriented
line direction.
For example, two, negative three, six and four, negative six, twelve are
proportional and describe parallel directions.
Multiplying by negative one reverses orientation but still gives the same
unoriented line.
The all zero triple is invalid because it provides no direction at all.
Zero in one or two individual components is allowed: a zero x component means
movement along the line leaves x constant.
To compare directions, proportionality must hold with one common multiplier in
all three coordinates.
Three arbitrary separate multipliers would make the test meaningless.
Avoid dividing component by component when a component is zero; compare
nonzero
ratios carefully or use cross multiplication.
A point and a nonzero direction determine a complete line, while direction
ratios alone determine only a direction and therefore a family of parallel
lines at different locations.
Direction cosines describe an oriented unit direction by its cosines with the
three positive coordinate axes.
If those angles are alpha, beta and gamma, write l, m and n for their cosines.
To obtain them from direction ratios a, b and c, divide each component by the
positive length square root of a squared plus b squared plus c squared.
For ratios two, negative three, six, that length is seven, so the direction
cosines are two sevenths, negative three sevenths and six sevenths.
Their squared sum is one.
The negative y component means the angle with the positive y axis is obtuse,
not acute.
Reversing orientation changes the signs of all three direction cosines and
replaces each axis angle by its supplement.
An unoriented line therefore has two opposite unit direction choices.
Ratios do not automatically satisfy the squared sum condition until
normalized.
If two direction cosines are known, the square of the third is one minus the
other two squares; its sign needs an orientation condition.
Check that this remainder is nonnegative before taking a real square root.
The dot product of two direction triples is the sum of the products of
corresponding components.
It equals the product of their lengths times the cosine of the oriented vector
angle.
For the smaller angle between unoriented lines, take the absolute value of the
dot product before dividing by the two lengths.
This chooses an angle between zero and pi over two and makes the result
independent of reversing either direction.
Two intersecting lines through the origin with directions one, zero, zero and
one, one, zero have dot product one and lengths one and square root of two.
Their smaller angle is pi over four.
A zero dot product gives perpendicular directions, while proportional nonzero
directions give a smaller angle of zero.
Check that both triples are nonzero before using the formula.
If a question specifically asks for intersecting lines, also verify they share
a point; a dot product alone does not establish an intersection in space.
Skew lines can have perpendicular direction vectors without meeting, so a
direction calculation and a position calculation answer different questions.
A line through point A with nonzero direction d has vector equation r equal to
A plus t d, with real parameter t.
This is compact notation for three parametric coordinate equations using the
same t.
Through one, two, three with direction two, negative one, four, they are x
equal to one plus two t, y equal to two minus t and z equal to three plus four
t.
At t equal to two the point is five, zero, eleven.
Substitution into all three equations verifies membership.
A candidate point must give the same parameter in every coordinate that
varies;
using a separate parameter for each coordinate would describe a larger set
than
the intended line.
The parameter is not generally distance travelled, because the direction
vector
may not be a unit vector.
Here a change of one in t moves a distance square root of twenty one.
Replacing d by a nonzero scalar multiple simply rescales the parameter, so
different looking parametric equations can describe the same line.
The base point A can also be replaced by any other point on that line.
Eliminating the common parameter from a line's three coordinate equations
gives
symmetric form when the direction components used as denominators are nonzero.
Through one, two, three with ratios two, negative one, four, write x minus one
over two equal to y minus two over negative one equal to z minus three over
four.
Every displayed quotient represents the same parameter.
A zero direction component must be handled as a constant coordinate equation,
not as division by zero.
For direction zero, two, negative one through the same base point, keep x
equal
to one and write y minus two over two equal to z minus three over negative
one.
If two direction components are zero, two coordinates stay constant and the
remaining coordinate varies freely.
A denominator in symmetric form is a direction ratio, not an intercept.
Multiplying all three denominators by the same nonzero constant preserves the
line, while changing only one generally changes its direction.
When checking a candidate point, retain the constant coordinate conditions as
well as the equal ratios, since omitting one condition can introduce points
outside the line.
Two distinct points determine a line in space.
Subtract their coordinates to obtain a nonzero direction and use one point as
the base.
For A at one, zero, two and B at three, four, zero, the displacement B minus A
is two, four, negative two.
The vector equation is r equal to A plus t times that displacement.
Thus x equals one plus two t, y equals four t and z equals two minus two t.
Parameter zero returns A, parameter one returns B, and one half gives the
midpoint two, two, one.
Restricting t to the closed interval zero through one gives the segment;
allowing every real t gives the whole line.
Direction ratios can be reduced to one, two, negative one, but then the
parameter values at the endpoints change unless the parameter is rescaled.
A third point is collinear with A and B exactly when its displacement from A
is
a scalar multiple of B minus A.
Coincident endpoints have zero displacement and do not determine a unique
direction, so the distinctness check is necessary before writing this
construction.
Two lines in space can intersect, be distinct and parallel, coincide, or be
skew.
Skew means they are neither parallel nor intersecting, so they do not lie in a
common plane.
To test an intersection of parameter equations A plus t d one and B plus s d
two, use independent parameters t and s and equate all three coordinates.
A solution must satisfy all three equations at once.
Solving two and ignoring a contradiction in the third gives a false
intersection.
For line one given by t, zero, zero and line two given by s, two, s plus one,
the y coordinates are always zero and two.
They cannot meet, and their directions one, zero, zero and one, zero, one are
not proportional, so they are skew.
By contrast, two proportional directions require a position test: if a point
of
one line lies on the other, they coincide; otherwise they are distinct and
parallel.
The equations t, zero, zero and two plus s, zero, zero describe the same x
axis
despite their different base points.
Unlike the plane case, nonparallel lines in three dimensions need not
intersect.
The closest point H on a line to a given point P is its perpendicular foot.
If the line is A plus t d, write H in that form and require the displacement P
minus H to have zero dot product with d.
Solving gives the foot parameter t zero equal to the dot product of P minus A
with d, divided by d dot d.
The denominator is positive because d is nonzero.
For P at two, three, four and the x axis given by t, zero, zero, the foot is
two, zero, zero.
The connecting displacement is zero, three, four, whose dot product with the x
direction is zero.
Its length is five.
If P already lies on the line, the foot is P and the distance is zero.
The vector formula using the cross product length of P minus A with d divided
by the length of d gives the same distance.
The projection method also supplies the actual foot coordinates, which a
distance alone does not provide.
Verify both line membership of H and perpendicularity of P minus H before
reporting the result.
For two nonparallel lines, their direction cross product is nonzero and
perpendicular to both directions.
Project the displacement between any chosen base points onto this common
normal.
The absolute scalar projection gives the shortest distance: absolute value of
B
minus A dotted with d one cross d two, divided by the length of that cross
product.
The cross product of triples a, b, c and p, q, r has components b r minus c
q, c p minus a r, and a q minus b p.
For line one t, zero, zero and line two s, two, s plus one, choose base points
zero, zero, zero and zero, two, one.
The directions are one, zero, zero and one, zero, one.
Their cross product is zero, negative one, zero.
The numerator is absolute negative two, so the shortest distance is two.
The expression is independent of the chosen base points and nonzero direction
scales.
A zero numerator for nonparallel lines means they are coplanar and intersect.
Parallel directions make the cross product zero, so this formula must not be
used in that case.
A shortest distance value does not by itself give the line carrying the
shortest segment.
To find the common perpendicular of two skew lines, let P be a parameter point
on the first and Q a parameter point on the second.
Require Q minus P to be perpendicular to both direction vectors.
This gives two linear equations for the two parameters.
For the lines t, zero, zero and s, two, s plus one, the connecting
displacement
is s minus t, two, s plus one.
Its dot product with one, zero, zero gives s minus t equal to zero.
Its dot product with one, zero, one gives two s minus t plus one equal to
zero.
Hence t and s both equal negative one.
The closest points are negative one, zero, zero and negative one, two, zero.
The common perpendicular has equation r equal to negative one, u, zero, with
real u, or equivalently x equal to negative one and z equal to zero.
The segment from u zero to u two has length two.
Verify that the line meets both original lines and that its direction is
perpendicular to each; those checks establish the geometry as well as the
algebra.
For parallel lines, the two direction vectors have zero cross product, so the
nonparallel shortest distance formula has a zero denominator.
Instead, use any nonzero common direction d and remove the component of B
minus
A along it.
The perpendicular component length is the distance.
Equivalently, take the length of B minus A cross d and divide by the length of
d.
For the x axis t, zero, zero and the parallel line s, three, four, the
shortest
connecting displacement is zero, three, four, giving distance five.
There are infinitely many perpendicular joining segments of this same length,
one at each matching x coordinate, rather than the unique common perpendicular
found for skew lines.
If the base displacement is itself parallel to d, the two lines coincide and
the distance is zero.
Always classify the directions first, then check location.
Nonparallel intersecting lines have distance zero but are not coincident.
A valid final answer should state which case applies, the distance, and any
closest points or common perpendicular equation the question requests.
Keep point membership and zero direction exclusions in that final check.
